name: Trinity Square
description: The main square of the Castle District, where Matthias Church, the Fisherman's Bastion and the Baroque Holy Trinity Column meet. The column was inaugurated in 1713 after a plague epidemic, and the square took its open shape only after the Ottoman rule ended in 1686.

children.text: Trinity Square, Szentháromság tér, is called the most significant square of the Buda Castle District by the district's heritage site. It lies where Tárnok, Szentháromság and Országház streets meet Hess András tér. Visit Buda Castle says the square, the richly decorated Holy Trinity Column, Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion together create a setting that invites photography and strolling.

It is not an old square. Until the end of the Ottoman occupation in 1686 a block of houses stood on the site. The Town Hall and the Nagyboldogasszony parish church, today's Matthias Church, were joined only by a narrow lane, with a row of houses directly in front of the church. After the houses were demolished, the church frontage became visible and the area between church and Town Hall was opened up. A spring-fed well with a statue of Pallas Athene, the town's defender, was completed in 1718.

The Holy Trinity Column is the square's centrepiece. The Council of Buda decided in 1694 to erect a column against the plague, the foundation stone was laid in 1700, and the first statue was finished in 1706. In 1709, during another epidemic, it was removed to the Újlak suburb. The present column was built between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713. The sculptor was Fülöp Ungleich, and Antal Hörger made the reliefs and coats of arms.

A hexagonal obelisk carries statues of Saint Roch, Saint John, Saint Christopher, Saint Augustine, Saint Joseph and Saint Sebastian, with reliefs of King David praying in repentance, the horrors of the epidemic in the Castle and the column itself. The Holy Trinity group crowns the top. The original sculptures are now in the Kiscelli Museum in Óbuda, and replicas stand on the monument.

Around the end of the nineteenth century the parish church was converted into a coronation church, the Jesuit buildings were cleared, and the former Ministry of Finance rose on the north side, opening the square towards the Fisherman's Bastion. The heritage site notes that the square's present form differs greatly from its Baroque layout because of replanning and reconstruction after the Second World War.
Good to know
Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion stand on or beside the square; check their official sites for visiting conditions and tickets.
Walk around the Holy Trinity Column to find the six saints and the three reliefs described above.
The square is the heart of the Castle District, so it is a convenient base for nearby sights such as the Hospital in the Rock and the Vienna Gate.

historyIntro: Trinity Square in the Buda Castle District took its open form only after the Ottoman occupation ended in 1686. Its Holy Trinity Column was inaugurated on 11 June 1713 as a thanks-offering after the plague.

historySections.heading: Houses before 1686 and the open square after

children.text: The Buda Castle District heritage site stresses that this is not an old square. Until the end of the Ottoman occupation in 1686 a block of houses stood on the site. Before then, the Town Hall and the Nagyboldogasszony parish church, today's Matthias Church, were linked only by a narrow lane, and a row of houses stood directly in front of the church. When these houses were demolished, the church frontage became visible and the space between church and Town Hall was opened up. In the eighteenth century the parish church was run by the Jesuits, with a monastery on the north side and a three-storey seminary on the south, and a Baroque Town Hall stood at the corner of Tárnok and Szentháromság streets.

The Council of Buda decided in 1694 to erect a Holy Trinity Column to protect the town from recurring plague, in gratitude for the end of an epidemic. The foundation stone was laid in 1700, and the first statue was finished in 1706 by the architect Ceresola Vereio and the stone carver Bernát Ferretti. In 1709, during another epidemic, it was removed to the Újlak suburb, and the magistrate ordered a larger and more decorative replacement. The present column was erected between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713, made by Fülöp Ungleich with reliefs and coats of arms by Antal Hörger. A spring-fed well with a statue of Pallas Athene was completed on the square in 1718.

Around the end of the nineteenth century the parish church was converted into a coronation church. The northern side of the church was cleared, the former seminary to the south was demolished, and the south-eastern side of the square opened towards the Fisherman's Bastion. On the north side the former buildings were cleared and the former Ministry of Finance was built. The heritage site shows photographs of the Jesuit convent being demolished around 1900 and of Matthias Church in ruins in 1945. It says the square's present form differs greatly from its Baroque layout because of town replanning and reconstruction after the Second World War.

name: St Elizabeth Church — Rózsák tere
description: The Roman Catholic parish church of St Elizabeth of Hungary stands on Rózsák tere in Erzsébetváros. Designed by Imre Steindl, the architect of the Hungarian Parliament, it has two 76-metre neo-Gothic towers, a richly furnished interior and a statue of the saint in front, from which the Square of Roses takes its name.

children.text: St Elizabeth's Church stands on Rózsák tere, the Square of Roses, in Budapest's seventh district, Erzsébetváros. It is a Roman Catholic parish church, and the parish gives its address as Rózsák tere 8. Its two towers, each 76 metres high according to Visit Hungary, make it easy to spot above the surrounding streets.

The building exists because the first church was too small. The independent parish of Erzsébetváros was founded in 1881 and built a modest eclectic church to plans by Győző Czigler, but the district grew quickly. A building committee was formed in 1889, and on 28 July 1892 the neo-Gothic design of Imre Steindl was accepted. Steindl is best known for the Hungarian Parliament Building, and Visit Hungary notes that visitors can see similarities between the façades of the two buildings.

Construction began in September 1893. King Franz Joseph I laid the foundation stone in person on 20 October 1895, and the church was consecrated on Ascension Thursday, 16 May 1901. Visit Hungary gives the floor area as 1,800 square metres and the capacity as 2,560 people, which explains why the church feels so large for an ordinary parish.

Inside, the furnishings were mostly made by well-known Hungarian craftsmen. Visit Hungary lists the main altar, the pulpit, the baptismal font, a Wedding Altar, the Altar of Archangel Gabriel, a Requiem Altar and an altar of St Anthony of Padua. Bombs hit the church in the Second World War; the parish says the damage was repaired by 1949, and a full renovation of the exterior and interior ran from 1995, with the exterior finished by 2004 and the interior by 2007.

In front of the church stands a statue of St Elizabeth by József Damkó, placed there in 1932 on the 700th anniversary of the saint's death. The square is named after the roses that are her traditional attribute. Visit Hungary dates the statue and the renaming to 1931, so sources differ by a year. On 29 April 2023 Pope Francis met poor people, refugees and charity representatives in the church during his visit to Hungary.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, rozsaktere.hu, or ask the parish for Mass times and when visitors can enter the church.
Look at the façade and towers from the square and compare them with the Hungarian Parliament, also by Imre Steindl.
Read the story of the roses before you go: Visit Hungary explains the tradition that gave the square its name.
Remember that the first, smaller church of the parish still exists as a separate building, now used by the Greek Catholic Church.

historyIntro: The church on Rózsák tere was built for a parish created in 1881 that quickly outgrew its first building. Its present neo-Gothic form dates from 1893 to 1901 and was designed by Imre Steindl.

historySections.heading: A parish and a church too small

children.text: The independent parish of Erzsébetváros was founded in 1881 by the Archbishop of Esztergom together with the city leadership. The faithful built a first, smaller church in eclectic style to plans by Győző Czigler, but it soon proved too small for the district. A church-building committee was founded in 1889, and on 28 July 1892 the neo-Gothic design of Imre Steindl was accepted; Samu Pecz and Sándor Aigner did not win the competition. When the new church was finished, the first one was handed over in 1905 to the Greek Catholic Church, and today it is the Church of the Protection of the Mother of God.

Digging of the foundations began on 23 July 1893, and construction began on 11 September 1893. King Franz Joseph I placed the foundation stone in person on 20 October 1895. The church was consecrated on Ascension Thursday, 16 May 1901. Steindl was also the designer of the Hungarian Parliament Building, and Visit Hungary notes that the façades of the two buildings show similarities. The same source gives the floor area as 1,800 square metres, the two towers as 76 metres high, and the capacity as 2,560 people.

historySections.heading: War damage, restoration and the Square of Roses

children.text: In the Second World War the church was hit by a bomb. Visit Hungary reports that the stained-glass windows were shattered, one arch was destroyed and the pedestal of the statue in the square was damaged; the parish says the restoration of the bomb damage was completed in 1949. A full renovation took place between 1995 and 2007, with the exterior completed by 2004 and the interior by 2007. In 1932 József Damkó's statue of St Elizabeth was placed in front of the church on the 700th anniversary of the saint's death, and the square was named Rózsák tere after the roses that are her attribute; Visit Hungary dates this to 1931. On 29 April 2023 Pope Francis met poor people, refugees and charity representatives in the church.

stories.title: The miracle of the roses

children.text: According to the traditional story told about Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, she was carrying bread to the hungry when someone stopped her and asked what she was hiding. Afraid she would be forbidden to continue her charity, she said she had roses. When she was made to show what she carried, the bread was said to have turned into roses.
This is a religious legend about charity, not a documented historical event. Visit Hungary notes that Elizabeth is often shown with a rose in her apron, and the roses give the square its name.

name: St Anne's Church — Batthyány Square
description: St Anne's is the Baroque parish church of Felsővízváros, the upper part of Buda's Víziváros, on Batthyány tér across the Danube from the Parliament. Begun in 1740 and completed in 1761 according to most sources, it is entered by steps down from the square, and the parish is known for its Jehmlich organ.

children.text: St Anne's Church is the Roman Catholic parish church of Felsővízváros, Upper Víziváros, at Batthyány tér 7 in Budapest's first district. English Wikipedia places Batthyány Square on the Buda bank directly opposite the Hungarian Parliament Building and describes the church as one of Budapest's most beautiful Baroque buildings. Its dedication is to Saint Anne.

The parish itself is older than the present building. According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the parish, it was founded in 1390, destroyed by the Ottomans in 1540 and re-founded in 1687, with baptismal registers starting in 1693. In 1724 the Buda city council bought a property on the site and had it converted into a chapel and parish house with a tower. The Jesuits served the parish, and as the congregation grew, work on a new church began in 1740.

The builder first commissioned was Kristóf Hamon. After his death, Máté Nöpauer of Brno finished the church in 1761, according to the same article. Wikidata records both men as architects and gives 1740 to 1761 as the construction period, while a caption on Wikimedia Commons dates the church to 1762, so the exact completion year varies by source. The Jesuits ran the parish until the order was suppressed in 1773; priests of the Esztergom archdiocese then took over, and in 1787 Archbishop József Batthyány split the parish in two.

A detail worth noticing is the level of the square. A We Love Budapest article on the history of Batthyány tér explains that landfill added in 1870, during the regulation of the Danube, left some older entrances below street level, so you reach St Anne's by going down a staircase rather than up. The same article places the church on the south side of the square, beside the market hall.

Inside, the parish website highlights the church's Jehmlich organ, which it describes as of European renown and recently repaired. The parish also runs a choir. The congregation was mostly German-speaking until the late 18th century, according to the Hungarian Wikipedia article, and the parish remains active today.
Good to know
St Anne's is a working parish church. Check the parish website, felsovizivaros.plebania.hu, for Mass times and for when visitors can go in.
Look at the steps down from the square: they come from the 1870 landfill described in a We Love Budapest article on the square's history.
Combine the visit with Batthyány tér itself and the view across the Danube to the Parliament.
If you are interested in the organ, the parish site lists music events and concerts.

historyIntro: St Anne's parish in Buda's Víziváros dates back to the Middle Ages, but the Baroque church seen today was built between 1740 and 1761 under the Jesuits. It stands on Batthyány tér, facing the Danube.

children.text: According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the parish, it was founded in 1390, destroyed by the Ottomans in 1540 and re-founded in 1687, and baptismal registers began in 1693. In 1724 the Buda city council bought a property on the site and had the mason master Henrik János Fiedler convert it into a chapel and parish house with a tower. The article itself notes that some earlier dates for the property conflict with the parish's foundation dates, so the early history is not fully settled. The Jesuits served the parish in the 18th century.

Construction of the church began in 1740 to serve a growing congregation. The builder commissioned was Kristóf Hamon. After his death, Máté Nöpauer of Brno completed the church in 1761, according to the Hungarian Wikipedia article. Wikidata lists both men as architects and gives the construction period as 1740 to 1761, and English Wikipedia says the church was built by the Jesuits between 1740 and 1761. A caption on Wikimedia Commons dates the church to 1762, so sources differ on the exact year.

historySections.heading: Parish changes and the raised square

children.text: The Jesuits ran the parish until their order was suppressed in 1773. Priests of the Esztergom archdiocese then took over, many of them former Jesuits, until 1803. In 1787 Archbishop József Batthyány split the parish, and the southern part became a separate parish under the Capuchins. The congregation was mostly German-speaking until the late 18th century. In 1870 landfill added during the regulation of the Danube left older entrances on the square below street level, which is why St Anne's is reached by steps down. In 1950 the reorganisation of Budapest moved the northern part of the parish area into District II and the southern part into District I.
